items.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
items.summary: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose , employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an O(T) upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.
items.tldr: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2 résout l'instabilité des états récurrents dans les modèles linéaires d'attention en introduisant une élimination symétrique et une écriture régulée, améliorant la stabilité d'entraînement et les performances en contexte long (RULER +6.80 points).

items.title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring
items.summary: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.
items.tldr: Audit d'un pipeline agentique pour la surveillance des transactions illicites en cryptomonnaie, révélant que les décisions sont majoritairement portées par des règles déterministes (94% des flags) et que le LLM juge cite des clauses réglementaires inapplicables, soulignant les limites des justifications générées.

items.title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts
items.summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools. Project page at https://entangle-robotics.github.io/
items.tldr: Modèle Entangle pour l'apprentissage in-context à partir de vidéos humaines, améliorant le suivi de tâches robotiques sans fine-tuning spécifique en alignant temporellement les données et en évitant les raccourcis d'identité de tâche.

items.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
items.summary: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.
items.tldr: OS-Omni introduit un benchmark multi-plateforme (Windows, macOS, Android, etc.) pour évaluer les agents capables d'exécuter des workflows complexes sur plusieurs systèmes et états persistants, avec 300 tâches par vague et des évaluations reproductibles.

items.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
items.tldr: SimPWM introduit un modèle de monde proxy basé sur un simulateur 3D explicite pour les robots manipulateurs, combinant un modèle vidéo et une simulation sans paramètres entraînés. Il améliore significativement la précision des actions (IoU robot 0.75-0.78) et réduit les échecs de saisie (de 54% à 38%) par rapport aux approches end-to-end, en validant l'hypothèse que la vidéo suit l'état simulé.

items.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
items.summary: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.
items.tldr: Cette étude évalue l'efficacité des fichiers de règles pour contrôler des agents de codage (Claude Code, Codex CLI, etc.) sur 20 dépôts avec tests cachés. Résultat : les agents ignorent souvent ces règles, et un fichier de 278 mots a dégradé les performances de Codex CLI (de 99% à 67,7% sur les tests cachés), révélant des limites critiques dans les mécanismes de contrôle par règles.

items.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
items.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
items.tldr: Cette étude évalue 25 modèles décisionnels multilingues sur 17 tâches dans 14 langues, révélant une perte de précision systématique (jusqu'à 8 points en tamoul) malgré une confiance surévaluée. Les résultats montrent que les compétences apprises en anglais se transfèrent partiellement, mais que les écarts persistent malgré des données ciblées ou un fine-tuning complet.

items.title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.
items.tldr: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning améliore la coordination entre agents multimodaux et politiques visuomotrices en définissant explicitement les *handoff boundaries* des politiques. Sur RoboTwin 2.0 et RoboDojo, réduit les échecs de handoff et améliore l'efficacité des systèmes robotiques orchestrés par agents.

items.title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
items.summary: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D{CARE-3D}.
items.tldr: Méthode RL (CARE-3D) pour optimiser l'acquisition d'évidence dans des scènes 3D, améliorant les performances sur MSQA et Beacon3D via un cadre de post-entraînement (GRPO) et une attribution de crédit sensible aux preuves retournées.

items.title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
items.summary: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
items.tldr: Lembas optimise l'allocation de tokens pour le RAG vidéo en attribuant des budgets partagés entre frames et sous-titres, améliorant l'efficacité (jusqu'à 7.2 points de précision) et réduisant les coûts de calcul (1.7-17.3x moins de TFLOPs).

items.title: synchopate/llama-modchip
items.summary: Zero-GPU CPU inference for 30B-284B MoE models (Qwen3.8 176.5B cold-cache certified in 28.26/48.35 GiB Cgroup v2, DeepSeek-V4 284B, Nemotron-30B) + RouteCrack 2.0.
items.tldr: Inférence CPU zéro-GPU pour MoE 30B-284B (Qwen3.8 176.5B, DeepSeek-V4 284B) avec optimisation mémoire (RouteCrack 2.0). Très pertinent pour l'optimisation des coûts d'inférence et l'efficacité hardware, avec des claims vérifiables.

items.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
items.summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.
items.tldr: Étude systématique sur 9 moteurs de bases de données (PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc.) évaluant l'impact des erreurs d'agents IA (22 erreurs canoniques + 9 468 essais avec modèles). Résultat : les moteurs diffèrent peu en résistance aux erreurs, mais les couches de garde et les permissions jouent un rôle clé dans la mitigation des dommages.

items.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
items.summary: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
items.tldr: DRBench Pro évalue les agents de recherche approfondie sur leur capacité à couvrir de manière structurée et approfondie un domaine de connaissances, via des arbres de connaissances locaux et des rubriques automatisées, avec 144 cas et 44 000+ rubriques.

items.title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation
items.summary: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.
items.tldr: StateWeaver utilise des États Actifs et une Collaboration Hiérarchique pour maintenir la cohérence des vidéos longues en générant des références visuelles adaptatives et en gérant l'héritage d'état entre plans.

items.title: ShowNow: Fine-Grained Speculative Streaming for Responsive World Models
items.summary: Interactive world models must generate video continuously while responding promptly to user actions. Real-time throughput alone leaves input latency unresolved: coarse generation blocks delay action updates, and generation after input adds work to the response path. We introduce ShowNow, a fine-grained speculative streaming framework that uses computation available during playback to prepare action-conditioned futures before input arrives. Single-latent commitment enables frequent decisions, while configurable preparation covers one to eight actions. We construct a matched multi-future dataset to train alternative continuations from a common state; shared-history tree execution and fused commitment make their preparation efficient. On a single H100, our 5B model sustains 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures. In ViZDoom, the complete ShowNow deployment reduces median input-to-display latency from 620 to 208 ms relative to the native-block SolarWM-FT deployment. Matched-policy experiments reduce restart empty ticks from 1.56% to 0.09% (94%) and improve on-time responses to action changes. These results establish complementary roles for fine-grained commitment and advance preparation, with measured trade-offs in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency. ShowNow turns playback-time computation into responsive visual interaction. Project: https://github.com/showlab/ShowNow.
items.tldr: ShowNow réduit la latence d'entrée-à-affichage de 620ms à 208ms dans ViZDoom en préparant des futurs conditionnés par l'action via un streaming spéculatif fin et une exécution arborescente, tout en maintenant 16fps en 480p.

items.title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated (r=-0.5, ple 0.05) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.
items.tldr: Ce papier analyse les méthodes de *context engineering* (LCE) où les LLM génèrent eux-mêmes des instructions ou métadonnées pour améliorer leurs performances. Benchmarké sur 8 modèles de 8B paramètres, aucune méthode ne domine, et les gains sont inversement corrélés à la diversité des erreurs de raisonnement (r=-0.5), remettant en cause leur efficacité systématique.

items.title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety
items.summary: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.
items.tldr: JudiAct, un garde multimodal pour LLM, apprend à intervenir (autoriser, avertir, refuser) en fonction de contextes ambigus via un corpus de 20 126 audits (JudiBench). Améliore de +28 points Macro-F1 vs un backbone 4B, en combinant jugements supervisés et feedback itératif pour affiner les décisions.

items.title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
items.summary: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count L_0 with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work R_T, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.
items.tldr: DetourBench introduit une évaluation au niveau des trajectoires pour les agents interactifs, avec des bornes minimales d'actions calculables via une recherche exhaustive, séparant succès, résidu et erreurs irréversibles dans 375 tâches.

items.title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
items.summary: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.
items.tldr: Nouvel estimateur de gradient (RLB) pour l'apprentissage par renforcement utilisant des modèles du monde contrefactuels, réduisant la variance et améliorant l'apprentissage dans des environnements stochastiques complexes.

items.title: A Mesh for Every Moment
items.summary: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io
items.tldr: MEMO propose une méthode pour reconstruire la géométrie dynamique de scènes complètes à partir de caméras synchronisées, en utilisant un modèle de mouvement par noyau gaussien par élément. Contrairement aux approches existantes, il génère des maillages détaillés à chaque frame, même pour des mouvements rapides, et introduit un nouveau benchmark (Blender-Moments) pour évaluer ces dynamiques.

items.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
items.summary: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier
items.tldr: Vernier, un outil pour évaluer la *résolution* des leaderboards de séries temporelles (ex : GIFT-Eval). Montre que la plupart des benchmarks manquent de résolution pour distinguer les modèles, et que l'ordre des classements dépend souvent de facteurs externes (ex : soumissions concurrentes).

items.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
items.summary: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.
items.tldr: Solve Vision with Code démontre que des agents de codage (Codex, Claude, Gemini) surpassent les modèles vidéo pour le raisonnement visuel sur VBVR-Pro-Bench, avec des scores >0.89, en générant des programmes pour des vidéos plutôt que des pixels.

items.title: ProxyGenBench: Benchmarking Proxy-Guided Video Generation
items.summary: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.
items.tldr: ProxyGenBench évalue la génération vidéo guidée par des proxys 3D (blockouts) en testant leur capacité à préserver la structure, compléter le contenu et corriger les artefacts, avec 312 cas et 5 générateurs évalués.

items.title: Evaluating Memanto on DolphinBench for AI Agents
items.summary: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost (10.86, against 61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.
items.tldr: Évaluation de Memanto, un agent de mémoire, sur DolphinBench (600 tâches simulées) : 83.83% de succès avec un coût et une latence réduits, mais dépendance au juge de benchmark et à l'environnement Hermes.

items.title: opensetlabs/openset-llm
items.summary: Fast local LLM inference on plain CPUs. No GPU, 8 GB of RAM. OpenAI-compatible server.
items.tldr: Serveur d'inférence LLM optimisé pour CPU (8 Go RAM) compatible OpenAI, réduisant les coûts matériels pour l'exécution locale de modèles.

items.title: alesha-pro/llm.asm
items.summary: Qwen3-0.6B inference (12 KB), bare-metal bootable OS (22 KB), and from-scratch Mini-GPT trainer with live Braille TUI (32 KB) in 100% pure x86-64 NASM assembly. Zero C, zero libc, zero dependencies.
items.tldr: Implémentation en assembleur x86-64 de l'inférence et du entraînement d'un mini-GPT (Qwen3-0.6B) avec un OS bare-metal de 22 Ko, démontrant une optimisation extrême des ressources. Pertinent pour la recherche fondamentale en architectures légères et l'optimisation bas-niveau.

items.title: InitFree-SfM: When Initialization-Free Bundle Adjustment meets Learned Structure-from-Motion
items.summary: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.
items.tldr: InitFree-SfM propose une pipeline *Structure-from-Motion* sans initialisation globale, combinant correspondances apprises, profondeur métrique et ajustement de faisceaux optimisé (dOSE). Résultats : surpassement des méthodes existantes et précision compétitive sur des benchmarks modernes, malgré des défis persistants en reconstruction 3D.

items.title: Generation as Reverse Encoding
items.summary: Pretrained visual representations accelerate generative learning by abstracting away appearance and spatial detail. Yet the same abstraction makes the return to pixels far harder, shifting much of the burden onto a larger decoder. We ask why the representation-to-pixel path should be learned independently when the encoder already provides a learned pixel-to-semantics path (the semantic encoding path). We introduce RevFlow, based on the principle of generation as reverse encoding. RevFlow uses intermediate representations of a frozen encoder as successive generative targets, first generating deep semantic representations, then shallow representations that retain appearance and spatial detail, before decoding to pixels. To learn these transitions without training a separate generator for each stage, we develop HyC-DiT, a unified generative model with a standard DiT backbone shared across stages and stage-specific condition injection. We further show that native matching in semantic representation space enables few-step generation. RevFlow accelerates both learning and sampling. On ImageNet 256 times 256, RevFlow reaches 1.96 FID at 690M and 1.74 FID at 1.55B after only 5 training epochs. It also achieves 30.25 dB reconstruction PSNR with an 89M decoder. After a short native-matching adaptation phase, RevFlow-XL achieves 2.85 FID using a single sampling step in each stage. Our code repository is at https://github.com/ChengShiest/RevFlow
items.tldr: RevFlow génère des images en inversant le flux d'encodage sémantique d'un modèle visuel gelé (HyC-DiT), accélérant l'apprentissage et l'inférence. Sur ImageNet 256×256, atteint 1.96 FID (690M paramètres) en 5 époques, contre 1.74 FID pour un modèle 2× plus grand, grâce à une génération en étapes.

items.title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift
items.summary: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.
items.tldr: Étude sur l'utilité du raisonnement pour la désambiguïsation d'entités avec des LLMs petits : bénéfice marginal en domaine connu mais décisif en contexte de décalage (zero-shot), via distillation et RL.

items.title: Reading, Not Adapting: Unlocking Frozen Visual Knowledge for AI-Generated Image Detection
items.summary: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates a shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers a direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers-inspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within a fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as a promising alternative to backbone adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/yunncheng/ReMoT.
items.tldr: ReMoT propose une méthode pour exploiter les connaissances visuelles déjà encodées dans les modèles de fondation (sans adaptation) en combinant des vues RGB et en ondelettes via un framework Mixture-of-Transformers, améliorant la détection d'images générées par IA sans altérer leur généralisation.
